Alright, there are a few things I should explain here before this whole thread gets any more full of yelling and screaming (hah, as if I could stop that).

First of all, contrary to popular belief, there are not a pile of servers hidden in some bunker labeled "the Internet central computers - do not touch" with a big red button and pressing that button will initiate the auto-destruct sequence on every Internet-based computer. This is not Star Trek and your computer will not explode (although with modern software I wouldn't bet on that being the case forever). Now, is this transfer a bad thing? You bet your ass. The DNS is not a thing to be trifled with. However, it's not quite so fundamental to the basic architecture of the Internet. It is equivalent to a centralized navigational system, but it is not the be-all and end-all, that being the main backbones that comprise the true core of the Internet. These are distributed among many stakeholders, at least right now, and many are already under the control of the governments that they happen to be stuck in. This is not a non-story but it is also not handing over control of the entire Internet to the international community, many of whom are far more corrupt and crazy than anyone in power in the US.

Second, the United States having control over the DNS does not mean that the "insane copyright industry" is going to have complete and utter control over all Internet communications. Don't get me wrong, I think the current copyright situation is reprehensible and will lead to ghastly long-term and short-term damage, and is actively causing it as we speak. However, that's not all there is to the story. If you take it out of the hands of the US, then you're going to end up with it in the hands of a lot of people with their own grossly corrupt agendas, and in many cases will also have their own copyright beef. Contrary to popular opinion, usually by those who think the US is the embodiment of all that is evil because it's the cool thing to say these days, copyright over-enforcement is a worldwide problem, which is part of what makes it so dangerous. Many aspects are especially bad in the US, but it is most certainly not only those in the US that benefit from it. There are bastards with vested interest in copyright overreach all over the planet, and the US is where it's most visible, particularly because it's in such stark contrast to freedom of speech, which is a Constitutionally enshrined right, unlike most places, even democracies.

Third, it's quite arguable the US did not have much of a choice. You can, in your basement, start up your own DNS root, and theoretically it could challenge and even overcome the ICANN root. The ICANN root is under de facto control by the United States primarily out of inertia and due to the fact that it has relatively reliably serviced the Internet since 1985 (ICANN didn't exist then, but the same root has carried forward). You can switch roots by changing a few numbers in your network configuration and maybe rebooting and it'll work. If this changeover was not done, then it would be done by every tin-pot dictator who had lackeys who could convince them that it might be a good idea to start up their own root and force their citizens to use it. Those who don't will probably stick out like sore thumbs, which is perfect for easy collection and "reeducation" via lead injection into the brain stem. As a note, there have been and still are competing systems for the root of the DNS. You can choose to use those. Unfortunately most people simply don't, so your chances of finding it useful are pretty slim unless you've got some kind of a niche you want to fill. If the US did not do this there was a good chance that a lot of other countries were going to do it themselves, which would likely result in people dealing with unfavorable governments having a lot tougher time of things because it would be that much harder to get their computer to access systems by domain names other than what their government provides. This would also provide little protection against terrorists or cyber-attacks, since anyone who wants to do those will almost certainly be able to access the ICANN root anyway, and possibly any other DNS roots they want.

This move is generally a bad thing because, for the most part, the DNS has mostly been left alone by the US, even though it is arguably under its control, or at least it was once control decentralized and third-party registrars started popping up (late 90's to early 00's or so, if I recall correctly). Now, the political sensitivities of despots the world over may well be reflected in its policies. Making putin-fucks-goats.com may get you put on a list (or obama-fucks-goats.com, or anything else along those lines). Don't get me wrong, there are people who have tried to over-control DNS as-is, and IIRC there have been a few domain seizures, but it's going to get much worse when anyone can stick their nose into the business of the DNS.

Many of the other countries who want this put under international oversight tend to want to adhere to the principle of self-determination. As countries. Not as individuals. The rights of the government, not the people who make up the governed, and unsurprisingly most of those individuals are not willing to die so that they can make sure that their president won't mess with how google.com is parsed on their web browsers, so don't expect armed uprisings there. That's the thing that a lot of people don't get, that this is not going to stop United States censorship, which is relatively speaking not as bad as most countries (hence why Voat is incorporated in the US - they researched it and put it in the US for that purpose) - it just means that everyone else gets to try to censor you too if they whine loud enough. So we get the clarity and freedom of expression demonstrated in the UN, along with the strength and efficiency of UN governance, all in one neat package.

Of course, that assumes any of this actually works out as planned. We all know how often plans go perfectly when involving actual human beings.

In short, this is a terrible development, but I'm not sure there was anything else to be done about it.

I'd put this in an edit, but I had a hard enough time getting the system to choke down my last spam ball of a post, so let me just tack it on as a comment to my own post:

The situation is NOT, however, HOPELESS, or anything like that. However, at the moment, there aren't any great alternatives. There may be alternatives in the future, such as a peer-to-peer DNS substitute, assuming the spam problem gets worked out. This is far from the first time such a solution has been proposed; in fact, it was brought up at least once in response to SOPA. Whether or not this might trigger its actual adoption is a question that cannot be answered at this time, nor can it be determined if this might give traction to other alternatives.

When I say "there is nothing else to be done," this is more along the lines of a governmental solution involving, specifically, control of ICANN and the ICANN DNS root. There are still other options, such as technological alternatives, but they rely on a large number of people adopting them to actually get much influence. Keep this in mind when considering your options for future technology use.

It's worth mentioning that ICANN also has control over IP addresses: they assign blocks of IPs to entities who then assign smaller blocks, etc. However, the exhaustion of the IPv4 address space poses an interesting possibility if we don't let the chance pass by: replacing a centralized address space with randomly-generated UUIDs. IPv6 provides more than enough room for this and has a low enough adoption at the moment to make such a transition with relatively little pain.

Meditation helps. Don't buy into that mystical, new age crap. Just practice deep breathing exercises at first, before you get into the actual meditation. here's one example, it's called "box breathing":

exhale all the air from your lungs, counting to 5

with no air, count to 5 again

inhale, count to 5

hold your breath, counting to 5 once more (when holding your breath, keep your airway open, don't close it off, if that makes sense)

My biggest trick for stress is journaling / free-writing. I just type what I'm thinking for a chunk of time each day; oftentimes it's boring ruminations and nonsense. But doing it tends to map out everything that's on my mind and give me great watchfulness over my thoughts 24/7. And from time to time, my writing will lead me to genuine insights, ways I want to change my thought patterns, or even uncovering deep-seated emotions. When the emotions come up, the urge is to distract or self-stimulate (e.g. watch TV, binge eat, fidget, get angry, etc.). The solution is to just sit and relax and feel the emotion. Some further insight might come then, about how you can address the situation; or it may be that there is nothing you can do and then you just have to accept the emotion as part of life and kind of be grateful that you are alive and able to feel.

The other important thing I am constantly reminding myself, I hinted at in the last paragraph. Anger can often be secondary to other emotions, and it can automatically be a way of self-stimulating to avoid feeling the primary emotion. For me, typically I am sad, and I get instantly angry before I even notice that it is sadness underlying it. A typical pattern then might be 1) sadness coming up 2) get angry 3) work out / exercise to burn off the anger. After that sequence, you're no better off than you were before since you just distracted yourself from the sadness. You did get a workout in, but this pattern can actually cause you to over-exercise and get run-down, but even worse is that you just steamrolled an emotion (in this case sadness) that you need to feel and process. Remember, "moderate" exercise. The truth is, anger is generally only useful if you are being attacked or confronted and really need to intimidate someone or physically defend yourself. Yes, you can channel your anger into things like exercise, but it is not very sustainable in the long-run. Ideally, you will exercise because you have good control of delayed-gratification and know that it will make you feel better throughout the week, for example, as opposed to exercising because you can't bear to sit still or because you want to punch a wall. I get angry so often and so easily, as a way to avoid feeling other painful emotions (mainly sadness), that remembering these things is huge for me.

Edit: Just wanted to add a better explanation of the first part. I think the way journalling works is it cuts down on worry-thoughts. Something about writing out your thoughts causes your brain to be able to inhibit going in circles. You've written enough that you are consciously familiar with everything that you typically ruminate about; you know all the dead-ends, the loops, and the thoughts that don't do you any good because they are about things outside of your control. Meditation works for this too in theory, but I find that writing is an easier option and often helps get me warmed up to potentially meditate. Oftentimes I'm so wired that I'll attempt meditation and be basically unsuccessful. Writing is always pretty easy to force myself to do, and it doesn't come with any of the confusion about what meditation is or whether you're doing it correctly. Just write as you think.
